title: Pain after surgery
intro: Some pain after an operation is normal, but it can usually be controlled well. Good pain relief helps you breathe deeply, move early, sleep and recover faster. Knowing the options and talking openly with the care team helps you get the right treatment with the fewest side effects.

sections.heading: Why pain relief matters
paragraphs: Poorly controlled pain can slow recovery, lead to chest infections, blood clots and weakness from staying in bed, and may increase the risk of long-lasting pain. Pain varies between people and depends on the type of operation, so your own experience is the guide. You do not need to be brave or wait until pain is severe.

sections.heading: Rating your pain
paragraphs: Staff often ask you to rate pain on a scale from zero to ten. Tell them how pain affects walking, coughing and sleeping, not just the number. Report new or suddenly worse pain, since it can be a sign of a complication.

sections.heading: Medicines
paragraphs: Treatment often combines several types of pain relief. Paracetamol and anti-inflammatory painkillers are the basis. Opioid medicines are used for stronger pain and can cause drowsiness, nausea, constipation and slowed breathing, and should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time. Local anaesthetic injections, nerve blocks, epidurals and infusions can numb the area.

sections.heading: Other helpful measures
paragraphs: Positioning, cold or warm packs, splinting a wound with a pillow when coughing, relaxation, music and distraction can help. Early gentle movement and breathing exercises reduce complications. Good information before surgery lowers anxiety, which in turn reduces pain.

sections.heading: Going home
paragraphs: Ask for a pain plan before leaving: which medicines, how often, when to reduce, and what to do for constipation. Do not drive or drink alcohol while taking opioids. Store them safely and return unused tablets to a pharmacy. Contact your doctor if pain increases, if you have fever, redness or discharge from the wound.

examples.title: Talking about pain
examples.text: Imagine you feel pain when coughing after abdominal surgery. You could tell the nurse that the pain stops you from taking deep breaths, and ask for pain relief before physiotherapy.

examples.title: Planning ahead
examples.text: Suppose your operation is next week. You might ask the anaesthetist which options for pain relief will be offered and how to manage side effects such as nausea.
